# Tidying Data with tidyr {#tidying-data-with-tidyr}

## Introduction

Tidy data has one row per observation and one column per variable. Real data
rarely arrives that way: metrics sprawl across columns, several values share
one column, and combinations go missing. In this chapter we reshape data with
**tidyr**:

- `pivot_longer()` / `pivot_wider()` — move between long and wide layouts
- `separate_wider_delim()` / `unite()` — split one column into several and back
- `drop_na()` / `complete()` / `fill()` — handle missing values and combinations

We will use the following R packages:








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(lubridate)
```
:::








## Data

We reuse the ecommerce data from @dplyr-basics, so no new data to learn.
The URL and date examples borrow the `mock_strings` and `transact` data sets
already used in @strings-in-r and @date-and-time-in-r.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ecom <-
  read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy/datasets/master/web.csv',
    col_types = cols_only(device = col_factor(levels = c("laptop", "tablet", "mobile")),
      referrer = col_factor(levels = c("bing", "direct", "social", "yahoo", "google")),
      purchase = col_logical(), n_pages = col_double(), n_visit = col_double(),
      duration = col_double(), order_value = col_double(), order_items = col_double()
    )
  )

ecom
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 1,000 × 8
   referrer device n_visit n_pages duration purchase order_items order_value
   <fct>    <fct>    <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl> <lgl>          <dbl>       <dbl>

 2 yahoo    tablet       9       1      459 FALSE              0           0
 3 direct   laptop       0       1      996 FALSE              0           0

 9 bing     mobile       3      19      209 FALSE              0           0
10 google   mobile       6       1      208 FALSE              0           0
# ℹ 990 more rows
```


:::
:::








## Long format with `pivot_longer()`

Suppose we average three metrics by device. The result is *wide*: one column
per metric, which is awkward to plot or rank.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
wide <- ecom |>
  summarise(across(c(n_pages, duration, order_value), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)), .by = device)
wide
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  device n_pages duration order_value
  <fct>    <dbl>    <dbl>       <dbl>
1 laptop    5.36     376.        441.
2 tablet    6.23     354.        352.
3 mobile    6.17     337.        370.
```


:::
:::








`pivot_longer()` stacks the metric columns into `metric`/`mean_value` pairs —
one row per device-metric observation:








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
long <- wide |>
  pivot_longer(-device, names_to = "metric", values_to = "mean_value")
long
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 9 × 3
  device metric      mean_value
  <fct>  <chr>            <dbl>
1 laptop n_pages           5.36
2 laptop duration        376.  
3 laptop order_value     441.  
4 tablet n_pages           6.23
5 tablet duration        354.  
6 tablet order_value     352.  
7 mobile n_pages           6.17
8 mobile duration        337.  
9 mobile order_value     370.  
```


:::
:::








## Wide format with `pivot_wider()`

The reverse trip is just as common. Counts by device and purchase come out
long (one row per combination):








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
counts <- ecom |>
  count(device, purchase)
counts
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 6 × 3
  device purchase     n
  <fct>  <lgl>    <int>
1 laptop FALSE      294
2 laptop TRUE        31
3 tablet FALSE      295
4 tablet TRUE        36
5 mobile FALSE      308
6 mobile TRUE        36
```


:::
:::








`pivot_wider()` spreads `purchase` into columns so each device occupies a
single row — the layout managers usually want in a report:








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
counts |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = purchase, values_from = n, names_prefix = "purchase_")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  device purchase_FALSE purchase_TRUE
  <fct>           <int>         <int>
1 laptop            294            31
2 tablet            295            36
3 mobile            308            36
```


:::
:::








## Split columns with `separate_wider_delim()`

The `url` column of `mock_strings` packs the protocol and the address into one
string, separated by `://`. `separate_wider_delim()` splits it into two
columns:








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mockstring <-
  read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy/datasets/master/mock_strings.csv')

tibble(url = head(mockstring$url, 3)) |>
  separate_wider_delim(url, delim = "://", names = c("protocol", "rest")) |>
  select(protocol)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 1
  protocol
  <chr>   
1 https   
2 http    
3 https   
```


:::
:::








The same verb splits calendar dates. The `Due` column of `transact` is
`YYYY-MM-DD`; splitting on `"-"` recovers the components:








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
transact <-
  read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy/datasets/master/transact.csv')

tibble(due_iso = as.character(head(transact$Due, 5))) |>
  separate_wider_delim(due_iso, delim = "-", names = c("due_year", "due_month", "due_day"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 5 × 3
  due_year due_month due_day
  <chr>    <chr>     <chr>  
1 2013     02        01     
2 2013     02        25     
3 2013     08        02     
4 2013     03        12     
5 2012     11        24     
```


:::
:::








## Combine columns with `unite()`

`unite()` is the inverse: it pastes several columns back into one. Splitting
the ISO date and reuniting it returns the input exactly — a useful check that
a separate/unite round-trip loses nothing:








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tibble(due_iso = as.character(head(transact$Due, 5))) |>
  separate_wider_delim(due_iso, delim = "-", names = c("due_year", "due_month", "due_day")) |>
  unite("due_rebuilt", due_year, due_month, due_day, sep = "-")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 5 × 1
  due_rebuilt
  <chr>      
1 2013-02-01 
2 2013-02-25 
3 2013-08-02 
4 2013-03-12 
5 2012-11-24 
```


:::
:::








## Drop missing values with `drop_na()`

`ecom` itself has no missing values, but joins create them: the full join of
`customer` and `order` from @joining-tables-in-r-dplyr carries `NA`s for
every unmatched row. `drop_na()` keeps only complete rows:








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
order <- read_delim('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy/datasets/master/order.csv', delim = ';')
customer <- read_delim('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy/datasets/master/customer.csv', delim = ';')

joined <- full_join(customer, order, by = join_by(id))
nrow(joined)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 349
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
nrow(drop_na(joined))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 55
```


:::
:::








Only the 55 fully matched rows survive — the same rows `inner_join()` returns.
Use `drop_na()` when a downstream step needs complete cases, and prefer it over
filtering each column by hand.

## Complete combinations with `complete()`

Counts over a filtered subset can silently omit combinations. Purchasers only
span `purchase == TRUE`, so the `FALSE` rows are missing rather than zero:








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
purchasers <- ecom |>
  filter(purchase) |>
  count(device, purchase)
purchasers
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  device purchase     n
  <fct>  <lgl>    <int>
1 laptop TRUE        31
2 tablet TRUE        36
3 mobile TRUE        36
```


:::
:::








`complete()` adds the missing combinations and fills the count with 0, so
plots and tables show every device × purchase cell:








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
purchasers |>
  complete(device, purchase = c(TRUE, FALSE), fill = list(n = 0L))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 6 × 3
  device purchase     n
  <fct>  <lgl>    <int>
1 laptop FALSE        0
2 laptop TRUE        31
3 tablet FALSE        0
4 tablet TRUE        36
5 mobile FALSE        0
6 mobile TRUE        36
```


:::
:::








## Fill down labels with `fill()`

Spreadsheet exports often write a group label once and leave the rest blank.
`fill()` carries the last non-missing value down (or up with
`.direction = "up"`):








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
report <- tibble(device = c("laptop", NA, "tablet", NA),
                 metric = c("aov", "orders", "aov", "orders"))
report |>
  fill(device)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 4 × 2
  device metric
  <chr>  <chr> 
1 laptop aov   
2 laptop orders
3 tablet aov   
4 tablet orders
```


:::
:::








## Your Turn

- reshape the mean of `n_visit` and `order_items` by `referrer` from wide to long
- split the `email` column of `mockstring` at `"@"` and reunite it — does the round-trip hold?
- run the `complete()` example without `fill`: what does the missing count become, and why?

## Try it in your browser

Edit the code below and press **Run**. It executes entirely in your browser
via [WebR](https://docs.r-wasm.org/webr/latest/) — no R installation needed.
The runtime downloads once, on this page only.
:::

```{webr-r}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
ecom <- read_csv("data-webr/ecom_sample.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
ecom |>
  summarise(across(c(n_pages, duration, order_value), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)), .by = device) |>
  pivot_longer(-device, names_to = "metric", values_to = "mean_value")
```
